title: Limited Efficacy of Benzocaine and Isoeugenol for Euthanasia and Humane Killing in Barramundi (Lates calcarifer) and Murray Cod (Maccullochella peelii)
content:
ABSTRACT

Methods for the humane killing and euthanasia of fish are key animal welfare practices for fish in captivity. However, recommended immersion anaesthetic doses used are often extrapolated widely across fishes with limited validation and variable success. This study evaluated the effectiveness of benzocaine and isoeugenol immersion as a method for euthanasia and humane killing in barramundi (Lates calcarifer) and Murray cod (Maccullochella peelii). Individual fish were placed in an aerated bath containing benzocaine (100–600 mgL−1) or isoeugenol (Aqui-S 150–600 mgL−1 with induction at 25 mgL−1) for 15 min and observed for excitatory responses, loss of equilibrium and cessation of opercular movement. Fish were then transferred to a clean, aerated bath for 60 min of observation. Barramundi recovered within 33 min when exposed to benzocaine concentrations up to 500 mg L−1 (n = 9) and within 42 min when exposed to isoeugenol at 400 mgL−1 (n = 3). Reliable death was only achieved in barramundi (n = 9) at benzocaine or isoeugenol doses of 600 mg L−1. All but one barramundi exhibited excitatory behaviour upon immersion into benzocaine or isoeugenol. Murray cod recovered within 6 min when exposed to benzocaine at 100 mg L−1 (n = 3) and within 25 min when exposed to 150 mgL−1 of isoeugenol (n = 3). Reliable death was consistently achieved in Murray cod exposed to benzocaine at 600 mgL−1 (n = 6) and isoeugenol at doses of 400 or 600 mgL−1 (n = 6). Loss of opercular movement is an unreliable indicator of death in barramundi and Murray cod. These findings add to the growing evidence of the limitations of anaesthetic overdose as a sole euthanasia method and indicate that the incorporation of a secondary physical killing method should be considered, while also highlighting the need for species-specific data to inform humane practices.
